\section{Data and Sample Details}\label{sec:app-data}
%======================================================================

\paragraph{Hours coding.}
The CBS records usual weekly hours in bins. Each bin is assigned its median ($4$, $11$, $18$,
$25.5$, $32$, $37$, $42$, $47$, $54.5$ and $78.5$ hours). The two irregular-hours codes are
imputed from observed medians within the same period. Mid-distribution bins are about five hours
wide, so the headline estimate, smaller than one bin width, is best read as a shift in the share
of women crossing a bin boundary. The 2017 file also codes reference-week absence differently.
Employed respondents absent from work that week were recorded at zero usual hours in 2017 and at
a real value from 2018 onward. Left uncorrected, this places roughly $5{,}200$ spurious zeros in
the pre-period. Because absence is more common among mothers ($12.4\%$ of employed mothers
against $7.3\%$ of childless women), the zeros fall unevenly across the two groups. Defining
hours on reference-week workers in \emph{every} year removes them and makes the hours population
identical across years, at a cost of about $10\%$ of each year's employed sample.

\paragraph{Reference-week absence and exposure.}
Absence is related to exposure. Among employed women with a matched occupation, the absence
shares by the quartiles of Figure~\ref{fig:dose-response} are $14.4\%$, $8.5\%$, $9.5\%$ and
$9.6\%$, highest in the least teleworkable quartile. After 2021 mothers' top-quartile share fell
from $12.1\%$ to $10.4\%$ and their bottom-quartile share rose from $15.5\%$ to $16.9\%$, while
childless women's top-quartile share is $6.1\%$ in both periods. Selection into the
observed-hours sample therefore includes movement across the absence margin, which is why the
bounds of Appendix~\ref{sec:app-lee} are defined on that sample.

\paragraph{Panel structure.}
The survey is a rotating panel. The $258{,}175$ reference-week workers of
Table~\ref{tab:descriptives} come from $64{,}602$ distinct respondents, about four observations
each and two to three within a single survey year. Repeat respondents account for $96\%$ of
rows. The regressions use $251{,}857$ of those rows from $63{,}199$ respondents; the $6{,}318$
dropped rows have a missing education code, the only control with missing values. Treating the
observations as independent would understate standard errors by a factor of roughly $1.8$, hence
the individual clustering of every DiD and every descriptive interval. The panel does not
support within-person identification. Of the $80{,}560$ women in the full sample, $1.9\%$ are
interviewed on both sides of the pre/post boundary, too few for an individual fixed-effects
design.
% Provenance: 1,514 of 80,560 distinct individuals (1.88%) appear in both the pre- and post-period
% (check_idpuf_panel_structure(), scripts/validation.R). The 6,318 rows with a missing education
% code (TeudaGvoha 99 -> NA) are the only listwise deletions: confirmed on cleaned_df.rds,
% 2026-09-23, with zero NAs in the other four controls on the hours sample.

\paragraph{Hours year by year.}
Panel~(a) of Figure~\ref{fig:hours-by-year} unpools the pre-period. The raw mother-minus-non-mother
gap widens monotonically across the three pre-period years, by $0.3$ hours in all, but each year
lies inside the others' confidence bounds. The post-period path is not monotone, and only its
2023 point, the year Section~\ref{sec:res-did} flags, is distinguishable from the pre-period.
The timing reading in the Discussion therefore rests on the event studies of
Figure~\ref{fig:pretrend}, not on this series.

\paragraph{Commuting.}
Mothers were the \emph{more} mobile group in every year. In 2019 they worked outside their
locality of residence $48.2\%$ of the time, against $46.1\%$ of childless women. Their commuting
also fell less in 2021: $1.5$ against $3.9$ percentage points, a difference of $2.39$ points
(SE $1.17$). This is consistent with remote work relaxing a time constraint for women who were
already commuting. It is descriptive evidence only, and no specification uses locality of work as
an outcome.

%======================================================================
\section{Exposure Construction}\label{sec:appendix-exposure}
%======================================================================

\paragraph{The external score.}
The Dingel--Neiman teleworkability score \citep{dingel2020} reaches the two-digit ISCO-08 level
through the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) crosswalk between ISCO-08 and the 2010 SOC
\citep{bls2012crosswalk}. Each
O*NET-SOC occupation in their classification is matched to every ISCO-08 unit group the
crosswalk lists for its six-digit SOC code. The score of a sub-major group is the unweighted
mean of their binary indicator over the matched pairs. Armed-forces groups have no counterpart
in their data and carry no score. The replication code re-derives the forty scores
(Table~\ref{tab:exposure-scores}) from the two public source files. Teaching (ISCO 23) is the
clearest case of a US task-based score misclassifying Israeli practice. It scores $0.966$ on
the external index, yet Israeli schools, closed and reopened in stages through 2020 and early
2021 \citep{somekh2021, hale2021}, were fully in person throughout the 2022--23 survey years.
Teachers did not work from home.

\paragraph{The calibration rule.}
The external score is replaced by the realized 2022--23 Israeli WFH share only where two
conditions hold. The gap between the two must exceed $0.5$, and a one-sided test at the 95\%
level, with standard errors clustered by individual, must distinguish it from sampling noise.
Ten of the forty two-digit occupations are swapped, among them teaching, clerical support
(ISCO 41) and ICT professionals (ISCO 25). Teaching falls from $0.966$ to $0.069$. The realized
shares pool men and women; Table~\ref{tab:robust} re-derives them from men alone. The realized
index reported as a bound is the realized Israeli WFH share by occupation, anchored to 2021
because no 2020 extract exists, with a minimum of 200 observations per occupation.

\paragraph{Masked occupation codes.}
The CBS masks some two-digit occupation codes for disclosure control. Those rows carry no
exposure score and drop out of the hours DDD\@. A partially masked code still identifies the
one-digit major group, so a proxy check compares realized WFH between masked and unmasked
employed women within the same major group in 2022--23. Among professionals (major group 2),
masked rows work from home at a share of $0.29$ against $0.16$ for unmasked ones, on $207$
masked observations. In the other major groups the masked rows are fewer and the gaps are small
or negative. Pooled across major groups, with major-group fixed effects and standard errors
clustered by individual, the masked-minus-unmasked difference in the share working from home is
$0.045$ (SE $0.021$) on $85{,}454$ employed women. The difference is significant at the 5\%
level and negligible in explanatory power (within $R^2$ below $0.0001$). The dropped rows are
therefore somewhat more teleworkable than those the index is built from: a small difference on
few rows, not a clean bill of health.

\paragraph{Fit.}
Across the forty occupations, on men and women pooled over 2021--23, the calibrated score has a
correlation of $0.53$ with the share who worked from home in the reference week. Its
occupation-size-weighted slope on that share is $0.40$ (SE $0.09$), so the score is relevant.
The raw external index fits better in levels (correlation $0.74$), because swapping ten
occupations onto realized shares while leaving thirty on task-based probabilities mixes two
scales. The calibration's contribution is not a better cross-sectional fit but the removal of
ten grossly mis-scored occupations from the treated tail. Table~\ref{tab:exposure-scores} lists
the external, realized and calibrated scores by occupation; panel~(b) of
Figure~\ref{fig:first-stage} plots the realized reference-week share against the calibrated
score.

\paragraph{Sensitivity to the swap threshold.}
Table~\ref{tab:calibration-sweep} refits the hours DDD with the calibration's swap threshold
moved from $0.30$ to $0.90$. Lowering it swaps more occupations and the estimate grows noisier.
From $0.75$ upward only teaching and clerical support are swapped. At $0.90$, above the largest
gap, nothing is swapped and the row is the external-index estimate of Table~\ref{tab:robust}.
The estimate is positive at every threshold. The step from the external index to any positive
threshold is the reclassification of teaching, which Table~\ref{tab:robust}'s teaching-only row
isolates.

%======================================================================
\section{The Selection Correction}\label{sec:app-lee}
%======================================================================

% tables/tab_lee_selection.tex and tables/tab_lee_bounds.tex are still generated by main.R
% (build_paper_tables()) but are no longer input here; the numbers below are quoted from them.
Let $s_{ab} = \Pr(\text{hours observed} \mid \Mother=a, \Post=b)$, the share employed and at
work in the reference week. Under parallel trends in selection, post-period mothers'
counterfactual is $s^*_{11} = s_{10} + s_{01} - s_{00}$. If $s_{11}$ exceeds it, the excess
share $1 - s^*_{11}/s_{11}$ is trimmed from their hours distribution, from the top for the
lower bound and from the bottom for the upper. One-tail trimming assumes monotone selection and
corrects only excess selection in that cell. For the DDD, counterfactual and trim are computed
within quartiles of the cell-based exposure index, which assumes that selection depends on
exposure only through the quartile. The model is re-estimated on each trimmed sample; for the
DDD, equation~\eqref{eq:ddd} is refit on the recombined sample with the occupation-level
regressor and occupation clustering. Each pair of bounds is reported with the Imbens--Manski
interval for the identified set \citep{imbens2004}.

For the DiD, $s_{11} = 0.696$ against $s^*_{11} = 0.683$, an excess of $1.9\%$. Trimming it
gives bounds of $-0.517$ (SE $0.178$) and $0.802$ (SE $0.179$) around the $0.228$ point
estimate, with Imbens--Manski 95\% interval $[-0.810, 1.096]$. The identified set and its
interval both straddle zero, so the DiD null survives the correction.

For the DDD the excess is present in all four quartiles but modest: a trim of $0.80\%$ to
$4.48\%$, or $1{,}396$ of $72{,}820$ post-period working mothers. The untrimmed estimate here
is $3.232$ (SE $1.054$) rather than Table~\ref{tab:hours}'s $3.224$, because this sample also
requires a matched cell-based exposure. The bounds, $3.126$ (SE $1.144$) and $3.443$
(SE $1.022$), lie within a quarter of a standard error of it, and the Imbens--Manski interval
$[1.021, 5.324]$ excludes zero. Under monotone selection, the gradient is not an artifact of
which mothers are observed working after 2021.

\section{Additional Results}\label{sec:app-results}
%======================================================================

Figure~\ref{fig:permutation} plots the reference distribution of the permutation test. Under the
sharp null the central $95\%$ of cluster-robust $t$-statistics lie between $-2.96$ and $2.60$,
and the observed $3.15$ is exceeded in absolute value by $31$ of $999$ draws.
Table~\ref{tab:extensive} reports the extensive-margin DiD and DDD discussed in
Section~\ref{sec:res-extensive}. Table~\ref{tab:balance-quartile} reports the pre-period
covariate balance between mothers and childless women within each exposure quartile of the hours
DDD's estimation sample, and Figure~\ref{fig:loo} the forty leave-one-occupation-out refits of
the headline estimate.
